why: The story never says whose bag this is. Holmes, not the Inspector, is the one who says 'In this bag I have...', so the 'Inspector's' attribution is not established.

text: One of the boots which Straker wore
why: Paragraph 101 states that Holmes has one of the boots Straker wore.
Paragraph 101 states that the bag holds one of Fitzroy Simpson's shoes.

text: A cast horseshoe of Silver Blaze
why: Paragraph 101 states that the bag holds a cast horseshoe of Silver Blaze.

text: When Silver Blaze cast the horseshoe in the Inspector's bag
why: The story gives no time for when the horseshoe was cast. The label supplies a point in time the story has not yet provided.

text: Whose footprints are in the mud of the hollow?
why: Paragraph 37 says the mud at the bottom of the hollow bears proof of who was there during the struggle, and the shoes and horseshoe now being examined give the reader reason to ask whose prints they are.

text: Whose footprints are in the mud of the hollow? — Straker's and the horse's only
why: Straker's and the horse's presence is established in ¶35 and ¶37. Whether anyone else was there is an open possibility the story has given reason to consider.

text: Whose footprints are in the mud of the hollow? — Simpson's among them
why: The police theory (¶46) places Simpson at the struggle, and Simpson's shoe is in the bag. Whether his prints are in the mud is a plain possibility the story has raised.

text: Whose footprints are in the mud of the hollow? — those of some third person
why: The story has raised other possible parties (the gypsies in ¶62, the Mapleton stables in ¶66, and the unidentified stranger), so a third person is a possibility the reader has reason to consider.
